generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shape holds across a surprising range of subjects, even where the methods look very different. Each part answers one question for the reader: what is being asked, how it was tackled, what was found, and what it means. When a piece of writing keeps those jobs separate, a reader can follow the project from its question to its answer without getting lost.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students write up the same small study, and we look at how each handles the parts.

{{learner-a}} opens by giving away the main finding, mixes an explanation of how the data were gathered into the results, and adds a personal opinion where the results should simply report what was found. The parts are all present, but they sit in the wrong places. A reader cannot follow the study from question to answer, because the structure is working against it.

{{learner-b}} lets each part do its own job. The introduction poses the question, the methodology explains how the work was done, the results report what was found without comment, and the discussion weighs what it means. A reader can follow the thread from start to finish, because the structure is doing the work.

Both wrote up the same study. Only {{learner-b}} placed each piece in the part that reports it.
generatedProse.summary: A research write-up has a recognisable shape: introduction, methodology, results and discussion, each doing its own job. Together they carry a reader from the question, through how the work was tackled, to what was found and what it means. You can now recognise the parts, and tell which one a piece of writing belongs to. With what research is, how a project is shaped, and the shape it takes, you have a map of research as a whole.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s write-up easier to follow than {{learner-a}}'s?

items.text: Each part did its own job: the question in the introduction, then the methodology, the results, and what they mean.
It was written in more formal, academic language.
It gave the main finding away in the introduction.
It included a personal opinion in the results.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} let each part do its own job, so the reader could follow the study from question to answer.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did with the parts, rather than the style of the writing.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s write-up was clearer because each part did its own job. Formality, giving the finding away early, or opinion in the results do not help the reader follow the thread.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
